title: Room for Revision
subtitle: A 25-minute documentary proposal for OpenAI about using Astra to plan, build, test, and account for a real rehearsal room
status: Development proposal. Planning is underway; field verification, construction and the finished documentary remain ahead.
deck: A working musician with no design or construction background pushes Astra through a poor first model, wrong assumptions, real records, buyable products, a $25,000 cap, trade validation, and the physical build. The errors stay in the film. The completed room, controlled performance, and paid invoices determine the ending.

sections.title: Follow the project from first prompt to finished room
sections.lead: The proposed film begins in the untouched room and follows the plan all the way through survey, trades, procurement, construction, commissioning, performance, and invoice closeout.

blocks.text: Greg Spero is a working musician and studio owner who began this room project without design or construction experience. He did know how musicians use the room, what a session needs, and when an image felt wrong. Through a long correction loop, he used Astra to turn an approved visual concept into an inspectable planning system: recorded geometry, editable 2D and 3D models, buyable furniture research, a line-item budget, trade scopes, material kits, ordered installation steps, and release gates for facts that still need people on site.

Proposed format: a 25-minute observational documentary, 16:9 master, clean master, full captions, transcript, trailer, cutdowns, production stills, and a public source appendix. OpenAI is asked to evaluate whether to follow or develop the story and to identify an editorial contact for a first conversation. If there is interest, TRC and a production partner would agree on access, production scope, editorial roles, distribution, and a quoted full-film budget. Production resources or support are an optional discussion, not a request approved by this document. No OpenAI participation, funding, or endorsement is claimed.

items: Room project cap: $25,000 all-in, separate from documentary financing.
Baseline price revision 1.7, checked 2026-09-28: $24,948.52 balanced; $24,953.78 ceiling-first; $23,257.16 with more cost protection.
The room ledger includes a $1,000 evidence-capture allowance for an archive and rough assembly. The finished 25-minute documentary needs a separate production agreement and quoted budget.
The final film is a completed case only after construction, commissioning, musical use, and cost records exist.

sections.title: A visible chain of responsibility
sections.lead: The camera can show where an agent expands a user’s reach and where authority returns to the person, the trade, the site, or the receipt.

items: Astra organizes records, compares sources, researches products, debugs geometry and code, generates or revises planning images, assembles budget logic, and keeps unresolved facts visible.
Greg decides the room’s purpose, musical use, taste, acceptable compromises, spending cap, and whether a result works for people in sessions.
Bounded GPT workers perform isolated research, extraction, implementation, testing, or review. Astra integrates and judges the work.
The approved September 13 concept came from Greg’s earlier room work with Claude. The film credits that source and does not present the concept as Astra’s original creation.

Qualified people measure, engineer or approve loads and attachment details, quote, fabricate, install, inspect, and commission. A model does not certify a wall, circuit, overhead assembly, or field fit.

blocks.text: The errors remain in the film because correction is the evidence. Viewers see a musician use an agent to plan beyond his formal training while keeping human control over taste, money, physical facts, and safety.

sections.title: Will the physical room accept the plan?
sections.lead: A musician pushes Astra past a bad first model and a beautiful but incomplete concept, then follows the resulting plan into a real $25,000 build where measurements, trades, receipts, and music decide what survives.

blocks.text: The stakes are already present. The first 3D pass is poor. The room shape and door assumptions change when old plans surface. The sofa direction changes after price, availability, shape, and fit review; the concept-faithful custom configuration still lacks a final dealer quote. Two raised storage-door platforms remain missing from the usable record and must be measured before fit can be released. The balanced budget comes within $51.48 of the cap. A wrong dimension can move furniture, change quantities, or stop custom work.

The ending stays conditional. If the room opens, the film compares the installed result with the model and records musicians using it. If a feature is deferred, the film shows the change and reason. If the build pauses, the documentary ends on the verified limit rather than manufacturing a reveal.

sections.title: Eight chapters from first prompt to paid invoices
sections.lead: Each chapter has something physical to observe, something exact to hear, and a record that turns the story.

rows: 1. The real room and the brief
Untouched room in normal use; locked wide; approved concept and earliest preserved conversation; natural room sound and a performance fragment.
The first exact prompt appears with its source. Earlier Greg/Claude concept credit is explicit.
2. Reject the model, correct the process
Poor early 3D against the real room; wrong orientation, generic forms, bad scale; exact corrections and version diffs.
The rejection moves Astra from visual polish to source records, editable geometry, and traceable revisions.
3. Put field truth into the geometry
Old plan, doors, booth, M-01–M-16 survey, and both raised storage-door areas.
A measured discrepancy updates the model and affected clearances or quantities. Unmeasured conditions remain holds.
4. Make the room buyable under $25K
Sofa candidates, tear sheets, furniture footprints, material rows, mirror and lighting kits, three budget options.
Source-backed products replace generic forms. The cap forces explicit choices while quotes and selections remain pending.
5. Give trades something they can challenge
Full-size mockups, samples, scope packets, redlines, trade questions, and bids.
Field facts and bids revise the package. Trades release physical methods; Greg approves scope and cost.
6. Build with Astra in the loop
Protection, deliveries, price proof, concealed conditions, fabrication and installation; crew photos and measurements beside versioned updates.
Each condition follows a visible chain: site evidence, plan comparison, trade decision, drawing/quantity/order/budget update, approval, installation, captured check, and as-built log.
7. Commission, correct, close the holds
Clearances, service access, lighting, AV cold start, appliance and ventilation checks, defect list, and corrected records.
Failed or changed checks update dependencies, punch list, budget, and as-built record. Open defects stay visible.
8. Music and receipts
Matched before/after, controlled performance, completed-room walkthrough, invoice ledger, and plan-versus-built comparison.
Paid invoices replace allowances. The close states planned and actual totals, approved changes, deferred work, and open defects.

blocks.text: Astra during construction is a proposed future workflow. It has not happened yet.

items: The crew submits labeled photos, measurements, delivery records, and the condition found.
Astra compares them with the versioned plan, identifies affected scopes, and requests missing facts instead of guessing.
The qualified trade chooses and releases the physical method, attachment, circuit, fabrication detail, or repair.
Astra updates the drawing, quantity, order tracker, budget, dependency, and change log.
Greg approves the cost and design tradeoff within the $25,000 cap before work or purchase proceeds.
The installer completes the work; the crew captures the check; Astra logs the as-built result, invoice state, and remaining holds.

sections.title: The project already contains the conflict
sections.lead: No producer needs to invent a crisis.

items: The poor first 3D has visible orientation, scale, shape, and relationship problems.
Room polygon, non-45-degree returns, doors, booth, and object axes change what fits and how quantities calculate.
A concept-faithful custom sofa has uncertain price, lead time, configuration, and orderability; lower-cost candidates compromise curve, arms, upholstery, or size.
The balanced package leaves $51.48 after current reserves; ceiling-first leaves $46.22; reserve-protected leaves $1,742.84. Accepted quotes may force deferral.
Two raised storage-door platforms need width, depth, height, edge, and door-clearance measurements before fit is released.
Mirror retention, overhead support, fire performance, electrical compatibility, backing, and final attachments require qualified trade or engineering judgment.
The budget is a planning ledger. Only quotes, purchase records, changes, and invoices establish actual cost.

blocks.caption: EARLY 3D / ITERATION. Hold on the flaws long enough for viewers to inspect them.

sections.title: Let the room and the records carry the film
sections.lead: No fake terminal typing, glowing AI interface, or omniscient model voice.

blocks.text: Lock one 4K 16:9 master camera before any room change and recreate it after commissioning. Record lens, height, distance, tilt, white balance, lighting state, and time-of-day window. Keep the before grade honest. Native screen recordings show source changes; cameras show Greg deciding, trades measuring, and the room changing.

items: Use five fixed evidence labels: RECORD, MODEL, VISUALIZATION, FIELD VERIFIED, PENDING.
Every cost carries its version and status: observed price, allowance, accepted quote, purchase, or invoice.
Build the soundtrack from room tone, tape pulls, laser beeps, keys, drums, saws, drivers, and relay clicks. Capture 60 seconds of room tone at every phase.
Do not grade the before footage to look worse. Do not substitute a visualization for installed-room photography.
Use native screen capture when a readable interface matters. Record Greg and trades with independent clean audio.

sections.title: Ask for examples, corrections, and limits
sections.lead: No one is asked to endorse Astra or OpenAI.

rows: Greg, before and after

What did the first model miss about using the room? What was visibly wrong? Which concept detail mattered most? Which source changed your mind? What would you refuse to order before a field check? What stayed, changed, or was deferred at the cap? What did the final model get right or wrong?
Lead builder or survey lead

Which pages helped you quote or sequence? Which assumptions failed at the tape? What required trade or engineering release? Which mockup prevented rework? Where did the documentation create work, and was it useful?
Glazier or millworker
What did the image communicate? Which dimensions, templates, substrates, loads, edges, and service needs controlled fabrication? What changed in the released shop drawing?
Electrician or systems installer
Which lighting or power assumptions survived? What did circuit condition, drivers, dimming, access, or code require? Which labels and tests will remain useful?
Musicians in the completed room
Can you set up, see one another, reach instruments, move, and use doors as intended? Which physical choice affects the session most? What still gets in the way?

sections.title: Shoot by milestone, protect the source record
sections.lead: The dates follow the real construction calendar. A missed moment is logged, not silently reenacted.

items: Phase A, now through survey: recover prompt history; lock story and source map; capture untouched room, first interview, native screens, and model versions; collect releases; photograph all surfaces and access points.
Phase B, trade development and procurement: film M-01–M-16, mockups, samples, redlines, scope choices, bids, final selections, quote revisions, and order releases.

Phase C, construction: capture demolition, deliveries, concealed conditions, inspections, changes, closure, installation, and commissioning. Seek 48 hours notice for irreversible events when the real schedule allows.
Phase D, closeout: matched final views, controlled performance, final interviews, punch list, as-built records, and actual-invoice review. Picture lock follows fact and rights checks.

blocks.text: Assumptions: local observational production, existing TRC access and archive, existing cameras and basic sound gear where suitable, eight to twelve milestone shoot days spread across the build, no celebrity fees, and restrained graphics. Greg contributes an estimated 30–50 owner hours for access, interviews, decisions, archive review, fact review, and approvals. Trade participation beyond normal project meetings must be quoted or agreed separately. Astra can prepare evidence maps, shot prompts, comparison scripts, transcript summaries, caption drafts, and fact-check lists through Greg’s existing account; that account use and Greg’s supervision are explicit contributions, not free production labor.

A production partner must quote the full-film scope after the construction schedule and crew plan exist. That future scope includes the listed paid hours plus local expenses, drives, transcription and captions, music or performance clearance as needed, insurance/admin where required, and postproduction. The full film is currently unfunded. Its budget is outside the approved $25,000 room project, authorizes no spending, and assumes no extra contribution from Greg. Travel, union requirements, delays, reshoots, original score, extensive animation, or a larger campaign would change the quote. The first OpenAI conversation asks whether the story fits an editorial or documentary program and who should evaluate it.
